title: Preface
summary: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.’s 2021 Form 10-K identifies the company, fiscal year, offices, incorporation and tax details, registered common shares and senior notes, filing status, filer classification, internal-control attestation, market value, outstanding shares, and proxy materials incorporated by reference. Its contents list covers business, risks, properties, legal and regulatory matters, securities and market information, management discussion, market risk, audited financial statements and notes, accounting and controls, governance, compensation, ownership, related-party matters, auditor fees, exhibits, schedules, and signatures.

title: Berkshire Hathaway Business and Workforce
summary: Berkshire Hathaway is a Delaware-based holding company headquartered in Omaha, with major insurance, rail, utility and energy operations plus diverse manufacturing, service and retail businesses. Its operations are highly decentralized; senior management oversees capital allocation, investments, executive appointments and governance, while the Board ensures CEO succession and the ethics code sets conduct standards. At year-end 2021, Berkshire employed about 372,000 people worldwide. Subsidiaries set their own workforce policies, commonly covering safety, compensation and benefits, wellness, training and advancement, and hiring, diversity and inclusion.

title: Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses

nodes.title: Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s global insurance subsidiaries insure and reinsure property, casualty, life and health risks, employing about 50,500 people in 2021. The text explains primary insurance and reinsurance, treaty/facultative and quota-share/excess contracts, competition, and U.S. and international regulation, including state oversight, NAIC and IAIS standards, group supervision, ORSA and capital tools. It notes Berkshire’s roughly $301 billion U.S. statutory surplus and strong ratings; outlines TRIA’s coverage, eligibility, deductibles and limits; surveys varied foreign requirements, operations and Brexit arrangements; and identifies GEICO, Primary and Reinsurance underwriting groups, their profit definition, pricing discipline and float-generating exceptions.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The text describes GEICO’s headquarters, subsidiaries, insurance offerings, distribution and service operations, competitive position, market share, pandemic-related premium credits, regulation, claims practices, and brand protection. It profiles Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group insurers, their coverage lines, customers, sales channels, and locations. It then outlines Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group’s global operations, market-dependent underwriting, and property/casualty and life/health businesses, including the NICO and General Re groups, their products, geographic reach, distribution, major agreements, and BHLN’s life and limited health reinsurance.

nodes.title: Berkshire Insurance and Reinsurance Operations
nodes.summary: GUARD provides commercial and homeowners insurance through agents and brokers; MLMIC specializes in New York medical professional liability. BHRG offers worldwide property, casualty, life and health reinsurance through the NICO and General Re groups, with business levels shaped by market pricing and large transactions. Property/casualty operations include NICO treaty, facultative and primary coverage, including an IAG quota-share agreement; General Re’s global treaty and facultative business, North American specialty insurers, and international operations through subsidiaries and Lloyd’s Syndicate 435. General Re also directly markets global life and health reinsurance. BHLN and affiliates reinsure traditional life, limited health, and certain closed-block variable-annuity benefit risks.

nodes.title: Insurance Products, Investments, and Float
nodes.summary: NICO’s retroactive reinsurance covers previously incurred claims, often with large aggregate limits and potentially substantial asbestos, environmental, and latent-injury losses. Pricing reflects the time value of money; expected underwriting losses are offset by investment benefits from premium funds. BHLN’s periodic-payment annuities fund long-term structured settlements, with discounted liabilities expected to accrete into underwriting losses. Berkshire’s insurance investments, managed primarily by its CEO, include concentrated public equities, fixed maturities, and cash, without targeted asset allocations or duration matching; equities have historically exceeded industry norms. Invested assets include shareholder capital and policyholder float, which rose from about $91 billion in 2016 to $147 billion in 2021. Float’s cost is measured by pre-tax underwriting loss relative to average float; it was negative in each year from 2019 through 2021 due to underwriting gains.

summary: The section surveys Berkshire’s global insurance and reinsurance businesses, their products, subsidiaries, distribution, competition, underwriting practices and regulatory environments. It describes GEICO, Primary and Reinsurance operations, including specialty, treaty, facultative, quota-share, retroactive, life and health coverage, major agreements and structured-settlement annuities. It also covers terrorism insurance rules, claims and brand protection, investment strategy and assets, and the growth and cost of policyholder float, including recent underwriting gains.

title: Railroad Business—Burlington Northern Santa Fe
summary: BNSF, headquartered in Fort Worth, operates a major North American railroad and a smaller logistics business, serving U.S. regions and parts of Canada and Mexico through major routes, shortlines, and carrier partnerships. Its 2021 freight revenues came from consumer, industrial, agricultural, and coal products; performance depends partly on economic conditions. Federal, state, local, and Canadian regulators oversee rates, routes, construction, acquisitions, safety, health, and hazardous-material transport. Extensive environmental rules, contamination liabilities, and operational risks affect costs. Diesel accounts for most baseline GHG emissions; BNSF targets a 30% reduction by 2030 through efficiency, renewable fuels, and evaluation of alternative locomotives. Competition from railroads and other transport modes pressures prices and service, prompting efficiency efforts; Union Pacific is its principal Western rival.

title: Utilities and Energy Businesses—Berkshire Hathaway Energy

nodes.title: Utilities and Energy Businesses—Berkshire Hathaway Energy (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire owns 91.1% of Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE), a global energy company whose locally managed subsidiaries generate, transmit, store, distribute and supply energy. Its regulated businesses include four U.S. utilities serving 5.2 million customers; five gas pipelines spanning about 21,100 miles, with 21 billion cubic feet per day of design capacity; electricity transmission interests; Great Britain distribution serving 3.9 million users; and Alberta transmission serving 85% of the population. Other interests include independent power projects, an LNG facility, major U.S. residential brokerage and franchise networks. BHE employs about 24,000 people.

nodes.title: General Matters
nodes.summary: The text outlines BHE’s utility and energy businesses: regulated electric and gas utilities in the western and central U.S.; Great Britain electricity distributors; Alberta transmission; interstate gas pipelines and storage; and renewable generation and tax-equity investments. It describes their service territories, customers, assets, energy sources, wholesale activities, and seasonal demand patterns. It also summarizes regulation: U.S. federal and state oversight, utility service obligations and cost-based retail rates, British distribution price controls, Alberta transmission regulation, and FERC and federal pipeline-safety rules governing gas pipelines.

nodes.title: Environmental Matters
nodes.summary: BHE faces extensive environmental laws covering climate, renewables, emissions, air and water quality, waste, and protected species, with ongoing compliance duties and potential penalties. Clean Air Act rules require emissions reductions at generating facilities; state renewable standards and possible clean-energy standards affect providers. The text outlines the Paris Agreement, U.S. withdrawal and reentry, and updated emissions and clean-electricity targets; the Clean Power Plan’s repeal, replacement by the Affordable Clean Energy rule, its court vacatur, and pending Supreme Court review; and growing state, local, and consumer clean-energy demands. BHE reports $30.1 billion invested in renewable generation, 16 coal units retired, and emissions down about 20% since 2005, with plans for further investment, 16 more retirements by 2030, and a 50% emissions reduction.

nodes.title: Non-Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America is the largest U.S. residential real estate brokerage, offering brokerage and integrated services such as mortgage, title, insurance, warranties, relocation and other home-related services. It operates about 900 offices across 33 states and Washington, D.C., with 46,000 agents under 55 brands. Its franchise network includes roughly 360 primarily U.S. franchisees and more than 1,600 international offices with 53,000-plus agents using two brands; franchisees pay fees for brand rights, training, advertising and related support. Revenue depends on home sales, typically strongest in the second and third quarters, and the business is highly competitive and sensitive to real estate market conditions.

summary: Berkshire Hathaway Energy (91.1%-owned) is a global, locally managed energy company with about 24,000 employees. Its regulated businesses span U.S. electric and gas utilities, British and Alberta electricity networks, and interstate gas pipelines and storage; it also has renewable generation, independent power projects, an LNG facility, and related investments. The section describes operations, service areas, assets, demand patterns, and federal, state, and international regulation. It covers environmental compliance and climate policy, BHE’s emissions reductions, renewable investments and retirement plans, and HomeServices of America’s brokerage, integrated home services, and franchise businesses, including their scale, revenue drivers, seasonality, and market competition.

title: Manufacturing Businesses

nodes.title: Industrial products
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s manufacturing subsidiaries are grouped into industrial, building, and consumer products and employed about 187,000 people in 2021. The text details industrial businesses: Precision Castparts’ aerospace, energy, alloy, casting, forging, fastener, and tooling products, customers, pandemic impacts, competition, raw-material sourcing, and environmental risks; Lubrizol’s additives and advanced-materials segments, markets, innovation, global operations, supply disruptions, safety investment, and regulatory and fire-related risks; IMC’s carbide cutting tools, operations, customers, competition, tungsten supply, and environmental compliance; and Marmon’s 11 diverse groups, products, locations, railcar and tank-container leasing, crane services, medical devices, and regulatory matters. It also describes CTB’s agricultural and food-processing systems, LSPI’s pipeline drag-reduction technology, and Scott Fetzer’s varied products and services.

nodes.title: Building Products
nodes.summary: The text profiles Berkshire Hathaway’s building-products businesses: Clayton’s homebuilding, financing, sales channels, backlogs, land holdings, supply and labor constraints, and regulatory obligations; Shaw’s flooring, turf and geosynthetic products, manufacturing, distribution, raw materials, and competition; Johns Manville’s insulation, roofing and fiber products, materials, facilities, environmental compliance, sales, competition, seasonality and sustainability; MiTek’s global markets, products and steel-supply exposure; Benjamin Moore’s paint brands, retail and online channels, competition, 2021 supply disruptions and environmental practices; and Acme’s brick and concrete products, facilities, markets, raw materials, seasonality and compliance with air-emissions standards.

nodes.title: Consumer Products
nodes.summary: The text profiles Berkshire’s consumer-products businesses: Fruit of the Loom’s apparel and sports brands, sales channels, manufacturing locations, raw materials, supplier concentration and disruptions, and competitive pressures; Garan’s children’s clothing and Fechheimer’s public-service uniforms; BH Shoe Holdings’ footwear brands and Brooks running products, sourcing and sales channels. It also describes Forest River’s recreational vehicles and other products, market share, competition and safety regulation; Duracell’s battery production, customers, market position and materials; Albecca’s custom framing products and services; and Richline’s jewelry and specialty-material business units and markets.

summary: Berkshire Hathaway’s manufacturing businesses are organized into industrial, building, and consumer products and employed about 187,000 people in 2021. The section profiles their products, markets, customers, operations, facilities, sales channels, competition, sourcing and supply constraints, and relevant business risks. Industrial companies span aerospace, chemicals, tools, rail and medical products, agriculture, and other goods; building businesses cover housing, flooring, insulation, structural systems, paint, brick, and concrete; consumer businesses include apparel, footwear, recreational vehicles, batteries, framing, and jewelry. It also addresses pandemic and supply disruptions, seasonality, safety, environmental and regulatory compliance, and sustainability.

title: Service and Retailing Businesses

nodes.title: Service Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s service businesses employed about 48,500 people in 2021 and span distribution, aviation, electronics, restaurant franchising, media and logistics. McLane distributes groceries, foodservice products and alcoholic beverages nationwide through three units, serving major retailers and restaurants. FlightSafety provides aviation training and manufactures simulators and training equipment worldwide. NetJets offers shared aircraft ownership, cards and related aviation services under extensive aviation regulation. TTI distributes electronic components globally to diverse industries and customer types. Other services include XTRA trailer and equipment leasing; Dairy Queen restaurant franchising; Business Wire news distribution; CORT furniture rental and sales; WPLG television; and Charter Brokerage logistics. Newspaper businesses were sold in 2020.

nodes.title: Retailing Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s retail businesses employed about 26,000 people at year-end 2021 and span automotive, home furnishings, jewelry, confectionery, kitchenware, party and educational products, and motorcycle goods. BHA operates 105 franchises at 82 U.S. dealerships, plus collision centers, auctions, distribution and vehicle/insurance products; its revenues are concentrated in Arizona, Texas and five major brands, amid intense competition and manufacturer agreements governed by franchise rules and state protections. Home-furnishings chains NFM, R.C. Willey, Jordan’s and Star operate large regional stores and distribution facilities, emphasizing value and cost control. Other retailers include Borsheims, Helzberg and Ben Bridge jewelers; seasonal See’s Candy; international direct seller Pampered Chef; multichannel retailer OTC; and European motorcycle retailer Louis.

summary: Berkshire’s service businesses employed about 48,500 people in 2021 across distribution, aviation training and services, electronics, equipment leasing, restaurant franchising, news and media, furniture rental, and logistics; its newspapers were sold in 2020. Retailing employed about 26,000 people and covered automotive dealerships and related services, regional home-furnishings chains, jewelry, seasonal confectionery, kitchenware, party and educational products, and motorcycle goods. Automotive operations face intense competition and are shaped by manufacturer agreements and state franchise protections.

title: Additional information with respect to Berkshire’s businesses
summary: The text directs readers to financial statement notes for Berkshire’s segment results, assets, and fixed-maturity and equity investments. It describes Berkshire’s 26.6% Kraft Heinz stake and Kraft Heinz’s global food and beverage business, plus Berkshire subsidiaries’ interests in four joint ventures or companies, with details in Note 5. It also explains that Berkshire’s website and the SEC provide free access to company reports and other materials, with reports available by written request to the corporate secretary.

title: Business Risks: Terrorism, Cybersecurity, and Key Personnel
key_items: General Business Risks Terrorist acts could hurt our operating businesses.
We are dependent on a few key people for our major investment and capital allocation decisions.
summary: Berkshire notes that known and unknown risks may impair its operations. Terrorist or other catastrophic attacks could damage facilities, systems, and personnel. Cyber risks include increasingly frequent attacks, operational and financial disruption, data and asset losses, remediation and reputational costs, competitive disadvantages, and difficulties raising capital, despite mitigation planning. Major investment and capital allocation decisions depend on Warren Buffett, with succession plans naming Greg Abel as a potential replacement; the Board monitors this risk, which is partly mitigated by experienced managers.

title: Key Business and Investment Risks
key_items: We need qualified personnel to manage and operate our various businesses.
Investments are unusually concentrated in equity securities and fair values are subject to loss in value.
Competition and technology may erode our business franchises and result in lower earnings.
Unfavorable general economic conditions may significantly reduce our operating earnings and impair our ability to access capital markets at a reasonable cost.
Epidemics, pandemics or other outbreaks, including COVID-19, could hurt our operating businesses.
Regulatory changes may adversely impact our future operating results.
summary: The page outlines risks from difficulty recruiting and retaining qualified personnel; concentrated equity investments losing value and weakening insurance surplus, ratings, and business capacity; competition and technological change eroding franchises; economic downturns reducing earnings and limiting affordable capital-market access; epidemics and pandemics disrupting operations, demand, supply chains, credit, and investments; and regulatory changes raising compliance costs or causing adverse effects, with privacy violations potentially damaging reputation and triggering penalties.

title: Risks in Regulated Insurance Businesses
key_items: Risks unique to our regulated businesses Our tolerance for risk in our insurance businesses may result in significant underwriting losses.
The degree of estimation error inherent in the process of estimating property and casualty insurance loss reserves may result in significant underwriting losses.
Climate change may impact our businesses.
summary: The company’s willingness to assume substantial catastrophe risk may lead to large losses despite underwriting controls; unexpected loss patterns or unenforceable policy limitations could undermine mitigation efforts and reduce earnings. Property and casualty reserves are inherently uncertain, take decades to settle, and even small increases in the $125 billion estimated unpaid-loss liabilities could materially lower earnings. Climate change may increase disaster losses, while climate-related regulatory noncompliance or reinterpretations could harm financial results.

title: Changes in regulations and regulatory actions can adversely affect our operating results and our ability to allocate capital.
summary: The text explains how changing regulations could affect Berkshire’s insurance, railroad, and utilities and energy operations, including limits on business, rates, capital, investments, dividends, emissions, and infrastructure decisions; compliance costs, hazardous-material liabilities, coal-market shifts, and restricted debt access may harm results, liquidity, or capital allocation. It reports no unresolved staff comments. It then describes BNSF’s extensive rail network across the U.S. and Canada, owned and leased track, operating facilities and equipment, approximately 7,500 locomotives and 63,600 freight cars, and about $2 billion in 2021 maintenance and repair expense.

title: Regulatory Risks and Railroad Properties
summary: The text describes extensive regulation of BHE utilities and energy businesses, potential financial effects of regulatory changes or noncompliance, and the substantial capital needs and financing risks of railroad and utility infrastructure. Item 1B reports no unresolved staff comments. Item 2 summarizes Berkshire’s physical properties, focusing on BNSF: its track network across the U.S. and Canada, operating facilities and equipment, approximately 7,500 locomotives and 63,600 freight cars, and about $2 billion in 2021 repairs and maintenance expense.

title: Utilities and Energy Businesses—Berkshire Hathaway Energy
summary: The text describes Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s electricity and natural-gas assets, supporting rights and debt encumbrances; lists generating sources, operators, locations, capacities, and 421 MW of facilities under construction; and outlines utility networks and gas pipelines, storage, and LNG facilities. It summarizes property types and owned/leased locations across Berkshire’s insurance, manufacturing, service, McLane, and retail segments. It also states that routine and other pending legal actions, including insurance and reinsurance claims, are not expected to materially affect consolidated financial condition or results.

title: Pipeline Systems, Other Properties, and Legal Proceedings
summary: Describes Northern Natural’s and Kern River’s pipeline, service-area, and storage systems. Summarizes Berkshire’s other segments’ property locations, facility types, and owned and leased property counts. Reports routine and other pending legal actions, including insurance-related claims and possible punitive damages, and states that resulting liabilities are not expected to materially affect financial condition or results of operations.

title: Executive Officers, Disclosures, Risks, and Shareholder Information
summary: Mine safety disclosures are provided in Exhibit 95. The page lists five executive officers, their ages, positions, start dates, and terms of service. It cautions that forward-looking statements are uncertain and identifies risks including investment and derivative losses, catastrophic events, epidemics, legal or tax changes, and economic and market shifts. Berkshire’s Class A and B shares trade on the NYSE as BRK.A and BRK.B; as of February 15, 2022, it had approximately 1,400 and 18,400 record holders, respectively, with nominees holding shares for beneficial owners. Berkshire has paid no cash dividend since 1967.

title: Berkshire Repurchases and Stock Performance
summary: Explains Berkshire’s repurchase program: Buffett and Munger may authorize Class A or B buybacks below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, in market or private transactions. Reports fourth-quarter 2021 purchases by month, share class, quantity, and average price. The program has no share or dollar limit, obligation, or expiration date, but repurchases cannot reduce cash, equivalents, and U.S. Treasury bills below $30 billion. The performance graph compares $100 invested in Berkshire from December 31, 2016, with the S&P 500 and property-casualty insurance index; index returns reinvest dividends, and the latter index is used because Berkshire’s diverse businesses make a peer group difficult to construct.

title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations Results of Operations
summary: Berkshire Hathaway reports after-tax earnings by business segment for 2019–2021, totaling $89.8 billion, $42.5 billion, and $81.4 billion, respectively; other earnings include goodwill and intangible impairment charges. The company describes its decentralized management and corporate oversight of capital allocation, investments, and operating-business leadership. COVID-19 sharply reduced many businesses’ 2020 earnings, followed by substantial recovery in late 2020 and 2021, while supply disruptions raised costs; future effects remain uncertain. Insurance underwriting earnings rose from $325 million in 2019 to $728 million in 2021, despite catastrophe losses, with results shaped by prior-year loss revisions, GEICO premium reductions, auto claims, and reinsurance. Insurance investment income declined in 2020 and 2021 as interest rates fell.

title: Results of Operations (Continued)

nodes.title: Insurance—Underwriting
nodes.summary: Railroad earnings rose in 2021 on higher volumes, revenue per unit and productivity, partly offset by fuel and volume costs; 2020 earnings fell amid pandemic-driven lower shipping volumes. Utilities and energy earnings increased in both years, driven by business growth, an acquisition, renewable-energy tax benefits and real estate brokerage. Manufacturing, service and retailing earnings rebounded in 2021 despite supply-chain input-cost pressures, after declining in 2020; pandemic effects varied by business. Other earnings included goodwill and intangible impairment charges, mainly a 2020 Precision Castparts impairment, and foreign-exchange gains or losses on debt. Investment and derivative results largely reflected volatile equity-market gains and losses that management considers uninformative about operating performance. Insurance underwriting is assessed separately from investing; investment income contributes to aggregate insurance results, while investment gains and losses are treated as non-operating. Catastrophes, reserve-estimate changes (including about $125 billion in unpaid losses at year-end 2021), and currency movements can materially affect underwriting results; notable 2021 catastrophes included Hurricane Ida, European floods and Winter Storm Uri.

nodes.title: Insurance—Underwriting (Continued)
nodes.summary: COVID-19 adversely affected some commercial insurance and reinsurance results in 2020–2021 through claims provisions, uncollectible premiums, and operating costs; future effects remain uncertain due to legal, regulatory, legislative, and economic factors. Berkshire’s insurance and reinsurance operations cover property, casualty, life, and health risks and comprise GEICO, Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group, and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group. The text reports group underwriting earnings, taxes, and effective tax rates for 2019–2021, and GEICO premiums, losses, expenses, and underwriting earnings. GEICO sells private passenger auto insurance nationwide, mainly through direct channels. Its 2020–early 2021 results reflected unusually low claims frequencies amid reduced pandemic driving, partly offset by higher claim severity and premium credits under the Giveback program; frequencies rose as driving resumed in 2021, while property claim severity increased with used-vehicle values.

nodes.title: GEICO
GEICO (intro)
nodes.summary: The text reviews insurance underwriting results for 2021–2019, noting COVID-related claims, uncollectible premiums and service costs, and uncertainty from future legal, regulatory and economic effects. It describes Berkshire’s insurance groups and reports aggregate pretax underwriting results. GEICO’s auto results reflect pandemic-driven changes in driving, claims frequency and severity, the Giveback premium credits, catastrophe losses, prior-year reserve revisions, premium and policy growth, and expense changes. BH Primary’s commercial and specialty premium growth, loss ratios, catastrophe and pandemic claims, reserve revisions, expenses, and long-tail liability risks are detailed. BHRG’s property-casualty and life-health reinsurance and annuity operations are also outlined.

nodes.title: Primary and Reinsurance Underwriting
nodes.summary: Describes BH Primary’s commercial insurance lines, major insurers and 2019–2021 underwriting results. Premiums written rose in 2021 across its insurers and increased modestly in 2020, partly offset by declines at other insurers and the Applied Underwriters divestiture. It reports loss ratios, catastrophe and pandemic losses, prior-year liability reductions, underwriting expense trends, and risks from severe, long-tail claims. It also outlines BHRG’s property and casualty reinsurance, life and health reinsurance, retroactive contracts, and periodic payment annuities.

nodes.title: Insurance—Underwriting (Continued) Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group (Continued)
nodes.summary: BHRG generally targets underwriting profits but expects losses on long-duration retroactive reinsurance and periodic-payment annuity contracts because deferred-charge amortization and discount accretion outweigh premiums’ investment income. The text presents 2019–2021 premiums and underwriting results by business line, then details property/casualty results: 2021 written premiums rose 6.4% on new business, participation, pricing and currency effects; 2020 rose 27.5%. The 2021 loss ratio fell to 71.9%, reflecting prior-year reserve reductions partly offsetting catastrophe losses; prior-year results included catastrophe, pandemic and reserve-development effects. Expense ratios and costs are discussed, including a 2021 ratio decline from mix and currency and 2020 expense growth with earned premiums.

nodes.title: Property/casualty
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group generally targets underwriting profits, but expects losses on long-duration retroactive reinsurance and periodic-payment annuity contracts because of deferred-charge amortization and discount accretion; upfront premiums are invested. The text presents 2019–2021 premiums and underwriting results by business, then details property/casualty and life/health results. Property/casualty premiums rose in 2021 and 2020; the 2021 loss ratio fell, with catastrophe, prior-year reserve, pandemic, and expense effects explained. Life/health premiums declined in 2021 due partly to a nonrenewed contract, but otherwise grew; pandemic-related mortality drove 2021 losses, while 2020 results reflected COVID claims and assumption changes, and 2019 included a one-time contract-amendment gain.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: The text reports retroactive reinsurance underwriting losses, foreign-exchange effects, prior-year claim-liability reductions and resulting earnings, plus unpaid losses and deferred-charge balances and their changes. It describes periodic-payment annuity premium trends, pandemic-related supply constraints, pricing sensitivities, underwriting losses, currency effects, mortality and interest-rate impacts, and liabilities. It gives variable-annuity guarantee reinsurance results and market drivers. It also summarizes insurance investment income by year, its decline due to low short-term rates, and the company’s preference for liquidity and safety over yield.

nodes.title: Annuity Underwriting and Insurance Investment Income
nodes.summary: Periodic-payment annuity premiums rose 16.3% in 2021 after falling 34.4% in 2020, reflecting pandemic-related settlement delays and sensitivity to pricing, interest rates, risk, and competition. These contracts typically incur discount-accretion losses; results also reflect mortality, interest, and currency changes. Excluding currency effects, losses were $526 million, $550 million, and $509 million in 2021, 2020, and 2019; higher mortality and interest rates partly offset 2021 losses. Liabilities totaled $15.1 billion at a 3.9% average discount rate. Variable-annuity reinsurance earned $114 million in 2021, versus an $18 million loss in 2020 and $167 million earnings in 2019, with volatile market, rate, currency, and margin-amortization effects; 2021 improvement chiefly reflected interest-rate changes. Insurance net investment income fell from $5.53 billion in 2019 to $5.039 billion in 2020 and $4.807 billion in 2021. Lower short-term and fixed-maturity income, amid persistently low rates, drove declines; the company prioritizes liquidity and safety over yield.

nodes.title: Insurance—Investment Income (Continued)
nodes.summary: Reports insurance investment income, including Berkshire Hathaway Energy preferred-stock dividends of $121 million in 2021 and $26 million in 2020, and a $365 million (8.1%) increase in 2020 dividends, mainly from Occidental preferred stock. Explains insurance float, its components and growth from $129 billion in 2019 to $147 billion in 2021; underwriting profits made float’s average cost negative for all three years. Provides 2021 and 2020 insurance cash and investment totals and 2021 fixed-maturity holdings by category, amortized cost, unrealized gains or losses, and carrying value. Notes U.S. government obligations’ AA+/Aaa ratings and that approximately 93% of foreign government obligations were rated AA or higher.

nodes.title: Railroad
nodes.summary: BNSF’s 2021 and 2020 results and freight volumes are compared with 2019. In 2021, revenue rose 11.6% and pretax earnings 15.7%, driven by higher volumes, revenue per unit, fuel surcharges, and recovery from pandemic impacts, partly offset by supply-chain disruptions. All business groups grew revenue, with explanations of volume and pricing drivers; operating expenses rose 10.2%, though the operating ratio improved, reflecting fuel prices and volume partly offset by productivity. In 2020, pandemic-related demand declines reduced revenue 11.3% and pretax earnings 6.3%; business-group results varied. Expenses fell 15.3% and the operating ratio improved due to lower volumes, fuel prices, cost controls, productivity, and better weather. The text details category-level expense changes and causes for both years.

nodes.title: Utilities and Energy
nodes.summary: Describes Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s ownership, regulated utilities, pipelines, renewable projects and real estate businesses; explains rate regulation and presents 2019–2021 earnings data. It details 2021-versus-2020 and 2020-versus-2019 earnings drivers for PacifiCorp, MEC, NV Energy, Northern Powergrid, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, brokerage, and corporate interest, including margins, volumes, weather, taxes, costs, acquisitions and regulatory changes. It also summarizes manufacturing, service and retail revenues, earnings, tax rates and acquisition/impairment exclusions, then breaks manufacturing results into industrial, building and consumer products.

Reviews Berkshire’s insurance underwriting and investment results, including GEICO auto trends, BH Primary commercial lines, BHRG property/casualty and life/health reinsurance, retroactive contracts, annuities, float, investment income, and portfolio holdings. It also covers BNSF railroad revenues, volumes, expenses, and operating performance, and Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s businesses, regulation, earnings drivers, and manufacturing, service, and retail operations.

It explains underwriting earnings, taxes, premiums, claims, expenses and investment income for GEICO, Primary and Reinsurance groups; COVID-19 effects, driving and claims trends, catastrophe losses, reserve estimates, currency movements, float, and investment holdings; and BNSF and energy-business performance, drivers and regulation. summary: Presents 2019–2021 revenues and pre-tax earnings for manufacturing and service and retailing businesses, along with income taxes and noncontrolling interests, net earnings, effective tax rates, pre-tax margins, and year-over-year changes. nodes.title: Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues (intro)
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents financial data for industrial, building, and consumer products, including revenues and pre-tax earnings for 2019–2021, year-over-year percentage changes for 2021 versus 2020 and 2020 versus 2019, and pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues. It is a continuation of Management’s Discussion and Analysis.

nodes.title: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing (Continued) Industrial products
Manufacturing, Service and Retailing (Continued) Industrial products (intro)
nodes.summary: The industrial products group comprises PCC (aerospace, power and industrial metals), Lubrizol (specialty chemicals), Marmon (over 100 manufacturing and service businesses, including equipment leasing), IMC (metalworking tools), CTB (livestock and agriculture equipment), and Scott Fetzer and LiquidPower. In 2021, group revenue rose 9.8% and pretax earnings 19.0%, with a 15.9% margin. PCC revenue fell 11.6% amid the uneven pandemic-era aerospace recovery, but earnings rose 78.8% following restructuring and lower charges; near-term aerospace growth is expected to remain limited. Lubrizol revenue increased 8.6% on pricing and slightly higher volumes, while earnings fell 50.8% due to a facility fire, impairments, higher input costs, and production disruptions. Marmon revenue rose 27.9% and earnings 40.3%, led by electrical, metal services, and plumbing/refrigeration, partly offset by divestitures and lower rail leasing. IMC revenue and earnings increased 19.5% and 47.7% on improved demand, efficiency, cost management, and currency effects. In 2020, group revenue fell 16.1%, earnings 33.4%, and margin declined to 14.6%. PCC revenue and earnings fell 28.9% and 64.5% due to pandemic-related aircraft declines and Boeing 737 MAX issues; it reduced its workforce about 40% and recorded $295 million in charges. Lubrizol revenue fell 8.0% on lower volumes and prices, while earnings were roughly unchanged as cost savings and insurance recoveries offset declines. Marmon revenue and earnings fell 8.2% and 24.3% amid weaker demand, lower metal and oil prices, divestitures, and restructuring; it acquired Colson Medical in 2019. nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: The building products group covers homebuilding and related finance, flooring, insulation, roofing, engineered products, masonry, paint and construction systems. In 2021 versus 2020, group revenue rose 17.6% to $3.7 billion higher and pretax earnings rose 18.6%; margins were nearly stable, amid strong demand and supply disruptions, constraints and cost inflation. Clayton Homes revenue and earnings grew, driven by home sales, financing and lower credit-loss provisions; site-built sales faced labor and supply delays, and loan balances increased. Other businesses’ revenue rose on higher prices and volumes, but earnings grew more slowly as input, freight, disruption, restructuring and impairment costs reduced margins. In 2020 versus 2019, group revenue increased 4.5% and pretax earnings 8.4%, with margins rising from 13.0% to 13.5%.

Consumer products includes recreational vehicles, apparel and footwear, batteries, framing and jewelry. nodes.title: Retailing
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s retailing segment is led by BHA, with more than 80 auto dealerships plus insurance, auctions and fluid products; home furnishings businesses account for another major share, alongside jewelry, candy, kitchen tools, party goods and motorcycle accessories. In 2021, retail revenue rose 19.8% and pretax earnings 76%, driven by stronger auto and home furnishings sales, margins and cost controls, despite chip-related vehicle shortages. In 2020, revenue fell 1% amid pandemic closures and supply disruptions, while pretax earnings rose 17.6%, supported by BHA and home furnishings gains; results varied among other retailers.

nodes.title: McLane Results and Investment Gains/Losses
nodes.summary: McLane distributes grocery, foodservice and beverage products, with high-volume, low-margin grocery and foodservice operations and significant-customer concentration. In 2021, revenue rose 5.6%, but pretax earnings fell 8.4% as labor, transportation, fuel and supply-chain costs outweighed sales gains; supply disruptions, shortages and higher costs hurt service and efficiency, and difficult conditions were expected to continue into 2022. In 2020, revenue fell 7.2% and pretax earnings 12.8%, reflecting pandemic restaurant closures, lower grocery sales, a shorter fiscal year, higher inventory reserves and foodservice losses. The page also reports 2019–2021 investment and derivative gains/losses, pretax totals, taxes and noncontrolling interests, net earnings, and effective tax rates.

Property claims generally settle faster, while casualty claims often have longer tails, sometimes lasting decades, due to litigation, contract interpretation, and legal processes.

nodes.title: Property and casualty losses (Continued)
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2021, consolidated claim liabilities, including retroactive reinsurance, were about $125 billion, 80% attributable to GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group (BHRG). BHRG’s unpaid-loss and adjustment-expense liabilities primarily arise from NICO and General Re. Excluding retroactive reinsurance, its 2021 totals were $38.239 billion gross and $37.166 billion net, comprising property and casualty case reserves, IBNR, and reinsurance recoverables.

It explains indefinite reinvestment of certain foreign earnings and potential taxes on distributions. It reports 2019–2021 tax expense by jurisdiction and current/deferred classification, reconciles effective tax rates to the U.S. statutory rate, and describes tax-return jurisdictions, audit years and status, unrecognized tax benefits, uncertain tax positions, expected examination settlements, and the lack of anticipated material tax changes or financial-statement effects.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements at December 31, 2021
nodes.summary: The notes summarize financial assets and liabilities at December 31, 2021 and 2020, comparing carrying values with fair values and classifying fair values by Levels 1, 2, and 3. Listed items include fixed-maturity investments, equity securities, Kraft Heinz stock, loans and finance receivables, derivative assets and liabilities, and notes payable and other borrowings. Cash, Treasury bills, receivables, payables, accruals, and other liabilities have carrying values considered reasonable estimates of fair value.

nodes.title: December 31, 2020
nodes.summary: The excerpt lists December 31, 2020 financial instrument fair values, including fixed-maturity investments, equity securities, loans, derivatives, and borrowings, with a note on balance-sheet classification. It explains the Level 1–3 fair-value hierarchy and reconciles Level 3 equity investments and put-option liabilities for 2019–2021, including gains, transactions, transfers, and ending balances. It describes the 2019 Occidental investments and reports 2021 Level 3 valuations, techniques, and assumptions for preferred stock and warrants, including duration, transfer restrictions, subordination, and volatility.

nodes.title: (21) Common stock
nodes.summary: The text presents Berkshire’s common-stock changes from 2018–2021, noting that 1 million preferred shares are authorized but none issued. It explains Class A and B voting, dividend, conversion, and single-class voting rights; equivalent-share counts for 2020 and 2021; and how average equivalent shares are calculated for earnings per share. It also describes the repurchase program: shares may be bought below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, without a set limit or expiration, provided consolidated cash, equivalents, and Treasury bills remain at least $30 billion; repurchases are not obligatory.

nodes.title: (22) Revenues from contracts with customers
nodes.summary: Explains revenue recognition when customers obtain control and presents 2019–2021 customer-contract revenues by segment and revenue source, distinguishing other revenue (mainly insurance premiums, investment income, and leasing). Reports remaining performance obligations at year-end 2021 and expected fulfillment timing for electricity and natural gas and other sales/service contracts. Describes defined-benefit pension plans, funding, and rate recovery; gives 2019–2021 pension expense components, unfunded-plan obligations for 2021 and 2020, and 2020–2021 reconciliations of benefit obligations and plan assets, including funded status, for BHE, other plans, and totals.

nodes.title: Revenue Obligations and Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Reports remaining performance obligations for electricity, natural gas, and other sales and service contracts, with expected satisfaction timing. Describes defined benefit pension plans, benefit calculations, contribution practices, pension expense for 2019–2021, projected benefit obligations and funding arrangements, unfunded non-U.S. and non-qualified U.S. obligations, and rate recovery. Provides 2020–2021 reconciliations of benefit obligations and plan assets, including funded status, for BHE, other plans, and totals.

nodes.title: Plan assets
nodes.summary: Reports revenue transaction prices for significant unsatisfied obligations due within and after 12 months. Describes defined-benefit pension plans, including expense components, funded and unfunded obligations, annual changes in obligations and assets, funded status, benefit obligations exceeding assets, actuarial assumptions, expected benefit payments and 2022 contributions. Summarizes pension asset fair values by investment type and hierarchy, investment objectives and return assumptions, and pension-related accumulated other comprehensive income changes. Also notes defined-contribution plan features and expenses for 2019–2021.

nodes.title: (24) Accumulated other comprehensive income
nodes.summary: Reports Berkshire Hathaway shareholders’ after-tax accumulated other comprehensive income changes for 2019–2021, showing beginning and ending balances, other comprehensive income, and reclassifications into net earnings for unrealized appreciation of fixed-maturity securities, foreign currency translation, defined benefit pension plans, other items, and the total.

nodes.title: (25) Business segment data
nodes.summary: The note explains Berkshire’s segment-reporting approach, including grouping similar businesses and reconciling segment results to consolidated statements; some intersegment transactions remain, while investment and derivative gains or losses, impairments, acquisition-accounting amortization, and other corporate items are excluded from management’s operating assessments. It lists activities for insurance units, BNSF, BHE, manufacturing, McLane, and service and retailing, then presents 2019–2021 segment revenues, pretax earnings, interest expense, and income tax expense, with reconciliation items and consolidated totals.

nodes.title: Business Segment Revenues, Earnings, and Taxes
nodes.summary: Presents three years of business segment data (2019–2021), including revenues and earnings before income taxes for insurance, BNSF, BHE, manufacturing, McLane, and service and retailing. Reconciles segment results to consolidated amounts through investment and derivative gains or losses, unallocated interest expense, equity-method investments, impairments, and corporate, elimination, and other items. Also reports segment interest expense and income tax expense.

nodes.title: Reconciliation to consolidated amount
nodes.summary: The notes present Berkshire Hathaway’s 2019–2021 business-segment data: revenues and earnings before income taxes, interest and income-tax expenses, capital expenditures, depreciation, year-end goodwill and identifiable assets, and reconciliations to consolidated amounts. They also summarize property/casualty and life/health insurance premiums written and earned, broken down into direct, assumed, and ceded premiums.

nodes.title: Business Segment Capital Expenditures
nodes.summary: Continued notes to the consolidated financial statements present 2019–2021 capital expenditures for Operating Businesses, with figures listed for Insurance, BNSF, BHE, Manufacturing, McLane, and Service and retailing, along with totals.

nodes.title: Reconciliation to consolidated amount
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports 2019–2021 consolidated reconciliation and year-end figures for goodwill, tangible-asset depreciation, and identifiable assets. It summarizes property/casualty and life/health premiums written and earned by direct, assumed, and ceded business, plus premiums written by geographic region. It also gives consolidated sales, service, and leasing revenue and its U.S. share; railroad, utilities, and energy revenue and its U.S. share; and the geographic location of net property, plant, equipment, and equipment held for lease.

nodes.title: (26) Contingencies and Commitments
nodes.summary: The company faces routine insurance- and reinsurance-related litigation, including occasional punitive-damage claims, and other legal actions that may involve fines or penalties; it expects none to materially affect its financial condition or results. Ordinary-course future purchase commitments, chiefly in railroad, utilities and energy, and aircraft ownership and leasing, total estimated payments of $34 billion from 2022 onward ($8 billion in 2022, $4 billion in 2023, $3 billion in 2024, $2 billion in each of 2025 and 2026, and $15 billion thereafter). Berkshire plans to acquire an additional 41.4% of Pilot in 2023, making it a consolidated subsidiary, and may acquire other noncontrolling interests; timing and cost depend on owners’ actions and interest values. Acquiring all such interests as of year-end 2021 would have cost about $11 billion.

summary: The disclosure reports 2021 mine-safety matters for PacifiCorp coal mines and Acme Brick clay, shale, and limestone facilities regulated and regularly inspected by MSHA.
